story.text: A school that is a Neighborhood Development Center with children in it. Written for Chris — RegenSonora Foundation, Leo's, and the Superior NDC — and therefore written for someone who already accepts the premise, so it spends its length on mechanism rather than persuasion.
## The argument in short

Superior is an unusually complete textbook for a town of 2,400. Within ten miles there is a copper ore body thousands of feet deep, a live sovereignty dispute that reached the Supreme Court, the oldest botanical garden in Arizona, a century of boom and bust, a bilingual mining culture, a creek, a tunnel, a legend, and a town that lost its hospital. Almost nothing a young person needs in order to understand the world is missing here. It is all at 1:1 scale.

A town needs an instrument that can see itself, decide together, and keep its own record. Almost no town can afford one, because it takes time, some neutrality, and a standing reason to publish. A school is the only institution a town already funds that has all three. Children have time. Children are the legitimate askers of naive questions — a fifteen-year-old can ask the water operator something a grown neighbour could not ask without it meaning something. And a school has a reason to publish that is not advocacy.

So the proposal inverts the usual relationship. This is not project-based learning, where the projects are simulations and a teacher grades them. The town actually needs the water record, and nobody is keeping it. The learning is a byproduct of the town's self-knowledge rather than a rehearsal for it. That is also the only version that survives contact with a real place, because invented projects rot within two years and real obligations do not.
## The commitment that makes it possible
The NDC school never enrols a student, never seeks a charter, and never applies for ADM funding. Its students belong to Superior Unified. Everything it builds is offered to the district to adopt.

That sentence is not a concession and it is not modesty. Arizona district money follows average daily membership, and in a small district anything that looks like it pulls students pulls dollars. Leaving the question open means every conversation with the district is secretly about whether we are a charter application in disguise, and they would be right to wonder. Closing it — publicly, permanently, in our own constitution, with a clause that can be made stricter but never looser — defuses most of the latent conflict before it forms and makes everything in [[Credit Ladder]] possible.
## The structure to plan on

The trap is writing a curriculum, because curriculum is a noun where a generator is needed. The plan has five planes, and curriculum is not one of them. Curriculum is the trace a learner leaves crossing them. See [[Curriculum Is A Record]].

- Commons — what is being learned about. The ore body, the creek, the ledger, the rules, each other. See [[Five Literacies]].
- Arenas — where learning happens. Campfire, cave wall, field, shop, meeting room, screen.
- Practices — the repeated moves. See one do one teach one, dialogue, measure, map, model, publish.
- Record — what persists. The badge ledger, the drawings, the datasets, the town's wiki, the paper.
- Constitution — who decides all of the above, and how that changes. See [[Seven Questions]] and [[Constitution Of The Gap Desk]].

Planes are for design. Ostrom's Institutional Analysis and Development framework is for analysis — when we want to understand a situation rather than build one, we use IAD, and the two are kept separate on purpose.
## Invariants, paths, and the record
A school can be self-organising and still be understandable, but only if three things are held apart.

- Invariants — the [[Five Literacies]]. What every graduate can do. Small, fixed, publicly argued.
- Paths — infinite, self-chosen, student-generated. No two look alike. See [[Ferndale Ideal Education Model]].
- Record — proof that some path covered the invariants, on a scale that can compare students who did nothing alike.

The third is the hard one and it is solved. Rasch measurement gives specific objectivity: the comparison of two people is independent of which items each of them took, provided the items sit on one ruler. A common curriculum is not required in order to have a common measure. That is the licence for everything else.
## What gets built first
The order matters more than the list, because each item earns the next.

- A record nobody asked for. The creek gauge, the rain gauge, the well levels, kept weekly, published, never missed. One year of it before anything else is claimed.
- A [[Gap Ledger]] in the wiki, with the school's own constitutions as its first entries, before anyone else's.
- The Ferndale map ported and forkable, so the first thing in the library is a demonstration that a student can make their own curriculum and hand it on. [[Eleven Steps]] is how the next person makes theirs, and it costs an hour and a pencil.
- One fire circle a month, tended by someone who has earned the badge. See [[Campfire Not Bonfire]].
- One thing given away, by every learner, every season.
## The honest difficulties

The school has to teach Oak Flat and Resolution honestly in a town where families sit on both sides. Not settle it. Host it. A school that can hold a contested commons without pretending it is uncontested has taught the one thing the wider world most lacks — and it is the reason the funding structure has to be solved before the curriculum, not after. If the mine funds the school, the school cannot hold that question, and everyone in town will know it.

Capture runs in both directions. If the district adopts our ledger, the district will want to control the ledger, and the entries about the district will be the first to quietly disappear. The protections are self-custodied identity, so a learner holds credentials no institution can revoke, and forking, so that any version of the ledger with entries missing is visibly a fork rather than the record. Both have to be in place at the start. By the time they are needed it is too late to add them.

story.text: The invariants. Five things every graduate can do, each anchored in a place you can walk to. They are the exterior curriculum, and they pair with the interior one in [[Ferndale Ideal Education Model]].
## Read the land

Why is the copper here. Apache Leap Tuff, the vein, the perlite still being dug, Picketpost, the Superstitions. Geology is time made visible, and the shafts are the only place most people will ever see thousands of feet of it at once. Mathematics comes out of this rather than being applied to it: scale, volume, the block-cave subsidence geometry, the three-dimensional problem of an ore body nobody can see. Boyce Thompson Arboretum is the living half — Sonoran upland ecology, drought adaptation, propagation, and the founding irony that the mine's founder built the garden.
## Read the water

Where does the tap water come from. Queen Creek, the wells, the aquifer, monsoon against drought, what Resolution proposes to draw and where the tailings go. Arizona water law is a full civics course by itself. This is also where measurement lives: the students keep the creek record, the rain gauge and the well levels, year over year, and learn what a control chart shows that a single number hides. A town that measures its own water is a different town.
## Read the ledger

Extraction economics at a scale you can see. What a mine job pays, what leaves town, what stays, what happened when the mine closed, what the town budget is, who owns the buildings on Main Street, why the hospital closed, what a festival is worth. Trace one dollar of copper from the rock to wherever it ends, then draw the counterflow — what came back, to whom, and how fast it left again. That second circuit is measurable, and a local multiplier study is an honest project with a real number at the end.
## Read the rules

Who decides what, at which level. Town council, school board, Pinal County, Tonto National Forest, the Forest Service, the San Carlos Apache and the O'odham, Congress, the courts. Students attend the meetings and map the rules in use rather than the rules on paper. This is the strand that cannot be taught anywhere but a small town where the rooms are open, and it is worked out in [[Seven Questions]].
## Read each other

Oral histories of the mining families — Mexican-American, Slavic, Italian, Cornish. The segregation the older generation remembers in these same schools. The strikes. The Apache Leap story, and how the Apache tell it against how the town tells it. Spanish and English as working languages rather than subjects. The film crews who came and left. What a community health worker does. How an elder is cared for when the nearest hospital is forty minutes away.
## What the invariants are for

They are not a syllabus and nobody teaches them as courses. They are the small set of things the community will check for, and the only claim they make is that a graduate who cannot do one of them has been failed by us rather than by themselves. Everything else a person learns here is their own path, and the paths are not supposed to match.
*Marc Pierson and Claude Opus 5 · September 2026*

story.text: In Ferndale in 2019, five students built their own curriculum over six weekly sessions. The artifact is a Plectica map titled IEM Plectica w/Labels: 232 nodes, of which 129 are concepts and 103 are link labels, joined by 167 links and grouped into thirteen regions. It is the best evidence we have that [[Curriculum Is A Record]] and that students can generate their own. The method that produced it is [[Eleven Steps]].
## What they built
Twelve domains, plus a High Level Connections cluster that holds all twelve as one densely linked network.

- Conflict — social pressure, expectations, drama, stories, social media, dealing with authority figures, overcoming obstacles
- Emotions — emotions we feel, love, heartbreak, dream concepts, trauma, hate, desire, peace
- Relationships — connections, people, love, friendships, relationships with family, selfishness, self love and respect, community, groups, awareness of external entities, open dialogue
- Happiness — travel, spontaneity, passion, greater acceptance, freedom, experiencing life, sunrises and sunsets, feeling empowered, expressing individuality, new challenges, purpose, abstract thought
- Health — environmental sustainability, diet, injury or illness, psychologists, first aid, mental health, exercise
- Development — home care skills, goals, problem solving, maintaining organisation, planning, work ethic, self-discipline, financial skills, cultural and social norms, emotion management, emotional development, loss and failure, accepting mortality, accepting change, existential experience, tragedies
- Academics — science, humanities, mathematics, technical skills, teachers, biology, psychology, chemistry, reading and writing
- Assets and Skills — wealth as time and choice, tolerance, cultural immersion, preparation for jobs, preparation for careers, cooking, money, control, external resources, time
- Guidance — opportunity, mentoring, books, an individual's navigation, parenting
- Perspective — belief systems, worldview, ethics and morals, pop culture, culture, perspective, experiences, media, fear concepts, sensibilities, history, politics, selfishness, art, environment, awareness, sustainability
- Scale — self, entities, big picture of life, individuality
- A Better Future — living comfortably, success, increase in community development, how to improve the community from home to world, cross-generational collaboration, posterity, happiness, balance, jobs in environmental development
## What the shape tells us

Perspective and Development are the largest clusters, at eighteen concepts each. Academics is nine, and it is the only cluster that reads like a school. It is also the most conventional and least interesting thing on the map. Everything else reads like a life.

They did not build a tree. The twelve domains carry fifty-four links among themselves, nearly complete and thoroughly cyclic — Conflict to Relationships and Relationships to Conflict, Happiness to Conflict and Conflict to Happiness, Emotions to Perspective and Perspective to Emotions. Adults asked to organise knowledge produce a taxonomy. These five produced a system with feedback in it, unprompted. That is the finding, and it is the argument for the whole approach.

Development is the cluster no school has. Loss and failure, accepting mortality, accepting change, existential experience, tragedies, with propositions such as tragedies teach good and bad about emotion management, and accepting mortality impacts existential experience. Teenagers put death in the curriculum. No district ever has.

The link verbs are the treasure. Most are ordinary systems vocabulary — is part of, allows, leads to, influences, creates, requires. Scattered through Emotions are four that are not: heartbreak envies love, dream concepts ignore hate, trauma listens to hate, desire admires trauma. That is poetry doing analytic work, and any adult ontologist would normalise it into relates to and destroy it. A modelling language that cannot hold envies cannot hold what a sixteen-year-old actually knows.

Two political claims arrived unprompted: selfishness creates politics, and history creates fear concepts. Selfishness is the one concept they placed in two clusters, Relationships and Perspective. They found it mattered twice.
## How it was made

Marc Pierson was introduced to Noah Williams, a disaffected high school student, midway through the first year of a Ferndale experiment: eighteen students who had given up on schooling, invited back as a cohort with one administrator, one facilitator and computer-based content, to educate themselves without a classroom and to come and go as they pleased.

The spread went through the student rather than the institution. Noah did [[Eleven Steps]] at Marc's kitchen table. Then the facilitator did it, separately, at the same table. Then her administrator did. Only then did the administrator and facilitator ask what could be next, and the answer was that Noah should invite four others from the cohort to do it simultaneously but separately.

Five personal drawings then had to become one. Six weekly sessions, sticky notes on a board, and the work turned out to be mostly about language: connecting nodes, long arguments about what words meant, renaming, a few additions, and combining near-synonyms.

That is the finding for our purposes. Integrating personal maps is not a diagramming problem, it is terminology negotiation, and it is slow. Six weeks for five drawings. Any design that assumes merging is a quick step after the fun part has the ratio backwards.

Marc held the same non-intervention through this phase, encouraging and neither judging nor suggesting, which is harder in a group than alone: what is being withheld is no longer the urge to teach but the urge to arbitrate. See the group rule in [[Eleven Steps]].

It also explains the duplicates. Selfishness appears in both Relationships and Perspective, Love in both Relationships and Emotions, Happiness in both A Better Future and High Level Connections. Those are not merge errors and not quite deliberate choices either — they are the residue of a negotiation where two people both raised a thing and nobody in the room had the authority to rule on it. The seams survive because the adult refused to settle the words. Keep them in any port; they are information.
## A caveat I had wrong

An earlier draft of this page said Plectica's built-in DSRP grammar shaped the output, because Scale, Perspective and Relationships read as three of Cabrera's four moves. That is probably wrong, and at most applies to the last step. The generation was analog — pencil, paper, sticky notes, eleven steps that mention no framework at all. Plectica was the transcription medium after the fact, not the thinking grammar. The clusters came out of six weeks of arguing about words.
## What happened next

Noah wrote the experience up and made recommendations to the administrator and facilitator, then built software to support community-based education of this kind. He and Marc gave a talk at Education for the 21st Century in Bogotá, where Marc met Kerry Turner, and ReLocalize Creativity came out of that meeting. Noah is now studying computational cognitive neuroscience in a self-constructed degree programme at Western Washington University, and flourishing.
Nothing stuck in Ferndale.

That is the most useful sentence in this page and it belongs in [[Credit Ladder]]. One student flourished and the institution did not change, because the work reached one facilitator and one administrator and then summer break arrived. There was no record the school had come to depend on, so there was nothing that made stopping costly. Ferndale is the evidence for why rung zero has to produce a record nobody asked for, before anything at all is proposed.
## Interior and exterior

What is structurally absent from the map is as informative as what is present. There is no place, no land, no work as such, no rules or governance beyond the word politics, no money beyond wealth and control, and no history except that experiences make up history.

Now set that beside the [[Five Literacies]]: land, water, ledger, rules, each other. They are complements rather than competitors. Ferndale mapped the inner world. Superior maps the outer one. The only overlap is reading each other, which is where both are richest and which no school subject covers.

A student's own curriculum is a path through both maps, and the school happens at the joins. Conflict meets the land exchange. Scale meets self, household, neighbourhood, town, watershed, county, state, tribe, nation. Guidance meets mentoring made structural. A Better Future meets the town's actual future, which is genuinely undecided. Development meets what happens when the mine closes again.
## What we still need from Ferndale

The map is the artifact. The generator is the method, and the method is not in the map. Who convened it, what the opening prompt was, whether the twelve domains came first or emerged from clustering loose nodes, how many sessions there were, whether an adult ever added a node, and what they threw away. That exists only in someone's memory or notes, and it is worth more to this design than the map itself.
## Porting it

The map should move into the RCN Graph Tool, and not as a copy. Three things are gained. Polarity and loops: their links are unsigned, many are plainly causal, and having students sign the edges and then find the feedback loops in their own map is a better systems lesson than any exercise. Composer levels: the twelve domains are the schema level, the 129 concepts the variable level, and one student's actual experiences the instance level, which is how a seven-year-old and a seventeen-year-old look at the same drawing. Federation: FedWiki gives four hundred forks with visible lineage, where Plectica gives one map with five authors.

The recommended build is a faithful port first, preserving their nodes, their terms and their unsigned links as the baseline everyone forks from, and then a signed causal version published as a visible fork of it. That costs one extra step and makes the first thing in the library a demonstration of the method.
*Marc Pierson and Claude Opus 5 · September 2026*

The seams survive because the adult refused to settle the words. Keep them in any port; they are information.
## A caveat I had wrong

An earlier draft of this page said Plectica's built-in DSRP grammar shaped the output, because Scale, Perspective and Relationships read as three of Cabrera's four moves. That is probably wrong, and at most applies to the last step. The generation was analog — pencil, paper, sticky notes, eleven steps that mention no framework at all. Plectica was the transcription medium after the fact, not the thinking grammar. The clusters came out of six weeks of arguing about words.
## What happened next

Noah wrote the experience up and made recommendations to the administrator and facilitator, then built software to support community-based education of this kind. He and Marc gave a talk at Education for the 21st Century in Bogotá, where Marc met Kerry Turner, and ReLocalize Creativity came out of that meeting. Noah is now studying computational cognitive neuroscience in a self-constructed degree programme at Western Washington University, and flourishing.
Nothing stuck in Ferndale.

That is the most useful sentence in this page and it belongs in [[Credit Ladder]]. One student flourished and the institution did not change, because the work reached one facilitator and one administrator and then summer break arrived. There was no record the school had come to depend on, so there was nothing that made stopping costly. ## Interior and exterior

What is structurally absent from the map is as informative as what is present. There is no place, no land, no work as such, no rules or governance beyond the word politics, no money beyond wealth and control, and no history except that experiences make up history.

Now set that beside the [[Five Literacies]]: land, water, ledger, rules, each other. They are complements rather than competitors. Ferndale mapped the inner world. Superior maps the outer one. The map is the artifact. The generator is the method, and the method is not in the map. story.text: The curriculum is what the student learned, or attempted to learn and the system failed them. Take that definition literally and the design of the school follows from it.
## A record, not a plan
If curriculum is what was learned, it can only be known afterwards. It is a record rather than a plan, and it develops with a person across the span of a life rather than being completed at eighteen.

The forward-facing object is therefore something else: an intention. A learner declares what they mean to learn and by when, and a mentor countersigns it. That is the dyadic contract, and it is the only part of the arrangement that points forward.
## The gap that unifies everything
An intention is a rule in form. The record of what actually happened is the rule in use. The distance between them is a gap, and it has exactly the structure the [[Gap Ledger]] applies to the town.

So the school keeps a gap ledger on itself, per learner. Not a gradebook. A ledger whose entries read: intended to learn to read the well log by March; did not happen; cause, the water operator was unavailable for six weeks and nobody arranged a substitute.

That is an institutional entry rather than a student one. The parenthesis in the definition — and the system failed them — becomes a data field with an owner. The failure is attributed to the thing that failed, publicly, in the same format the newspaper uses on the town council.

A school willing to publish its own gap ledger has earned the standing to publish anyone else's. It also puts the method in the same place as the subject matter, because students learn gap analysis by having it run honestly on their own school, about them, where they can read it and argue with it.
One instrument, three scopes: the learner's own intentions, the school's constitutions, and the town's rules.
## The record includes how it felt

[[Eleven Steps]] devotes half its length to recalling, out loud, how each earlier step felt, and says plainly that this is where the big learning is. That is not a wellbeing add-on, it is the part of the record a gradebook cannot hold.

So a learner's record carries two tracks. What was made, which is the artifact and the badge. And what it was like to make it, in their own words, written down at the time. The second is what tells a person years later why a whole class of work felt closed to them, and it is the only evidence that can distinguish did not from would not from was not allowed to.
Every step of the protocol carries a Notes field from the beginning rather than a reflection tacked on at the end, and our ledger should be built the same way.
## Every student generates their own

[[Ferndale Ideal Education Model]] is the evidence that this is not aspirational, and [[Eleven Steps]] is the method. Curriculum-making is itself the first curriculum, and it recurs. Each season a student publishes a map of what they intend to learn and why, in the graph tool, on the wiki.

Because it is FedWiki, a curriculum is a page you fork. Within a few years the school holds hundreds of student-authored, forked and mutated curricula whose lineage is visible, and that library will be better than anything the adults would have written. The adults stop assigning and start watching the aggregate for invariants nobody is choosing, and then offering.
## How progress stays legible
Two readings of one ledger, on one picture.

- The student's own standard is the declared intention, countersigned. It appears on the map as the learner's own marker.
- The community's standard is a threshold the town draws on the same ruler and argues about in public — to be trusted with the water record you need to be here. That cut is a collective-choice decision rather than a psychometric one. It is contestable and amendable, and putting it where the town sets it is more honest than any state cut score.

Rasch measurement is what makes both readable at once. Persons on the left of a Wright map, items on the right, both on the same scale. A student sees exactly which badges sit just above their current position, which is the zone of proximal development rendered as a map rather than a metaphor. A ten-year-old can read it. One Wright map is the whole transcript.

See one, do one, teach one supplies the item structure for free, because teaching is strictly harder than doing, so each competence yields an ordered three-threshold item. The teach step is also the validity check, since nobody can fake teaching in front of the person who taught them. Verification is human and situated rather than proctored.

Misfit is the good data. Someone who earns a hard badge having skipped easy ones is either a mis-calibrated item or a genuinely unusual path, and in a standardised school that is noise to suppress while here it is the most interesting row in the table and worth a conversation.

Two cautions, stated once. Rasch assumes one dimension, so more than one ruler will probably be needed — something like reading the land, making, and dialogue and governance — rather than pretending to a single achievement score. And badge difficulties are estimated from the data, so in the first year with few people they are noisy, and the map should be published as provisional and said to be provisional.
## What replaces grades and classes
Three couplings are cut separately.

- Age to cohort, cut by see one do one teach one. The teacher is whoever holds the badge, so a twelve-year-old teaching a forty-year-old the well log is unremarkable. Mixed age is the mechanism rather than a concession.
- Subject to period to room, cut by rhythm rather than schedule. A day has a shape — morning circle, long field block, making block, publish before dark — not eight bells. Rooms are named for what is made in them: map room, shop, bench, booth, kitchen, quiet room. Nothing is called a classroom. Outside is the default, with the seasonal inversion Superior forces anyway, outdoors early and late in summer and midday in winter.
- Level to graduation, cut by continuous thresholds on one public ruler. Nobody is promoted in June. People cross thresholds whenever they cross them, and the completion of a piece of work is that it is given away.
*Marc Pierson and Claude Opus 5 · September 2026*

story.text: Elinor Ostrom's working rule types, put as questions a nine-year-old can ask of any situation — a town council, a grazing permit, a family, a basketball game, a project crew.
## The questions

- Boundary. Who is in and who is out. How do you get in. How do you get out.
- Position. What roles exist here. Roles rather than people, because the role outlives the person.
- Choice. What is each role allowed to do, required to do, forbidden to do.
- Aggregation. How do we decide. Who has to agree for it to count.
- Information. What has to be shared, with whom, and when. What may be kept quiet.
- Payoff. Who bears the cost and who gets the benefit. What happens if you break it.
- Scope. What outcomes are we allowed to affect. What is off limits.

Aggregation is the one to install first and hardest, from about age six, at the level of who picks the game. Most conflict is two people silently assuming different aggregation rules. A tool that takes one decision, one set of positions, and shows what each aggregation rule would have produced from the same inputs teaches more about politics than a year of the subject.
## The three levels
Operational rules govern day-to-day action in an arena — who takes water, who repairs the fence, who speaks, who gets the permit. Changing one is cheap and frequent.
Collective-choice rules say who is entitled to change the operational rules, and by what procedure. Council votes, board policy, permit conditions, a union contract, the bylaws of a water co-op.
Constitutional rules say who is entitled to change the collective-choice rules. Charters, a district's authorising law, a land exchange statute, treaty status, incorporation.
Beneath all three is the meta-constitutional level — culture, what people believe is even thinkable. It is unwritten, which is why it is the strongest.

The same seven rule types operate at every level, which is what makes the questions general rather than a civics lesson. And the gap between rules in form and rules in use is the actual subject matter, findable only by observation — sitting in the room, walking the allotment, asking the clerk. That is the part no online course can do and a Superior school can do trivially.

Mapped to Donella Meadows: operational sits at leverage points twelve through seven, collective-choice at six and five, constitutional at four through one. That tells you which tool to reach for at each level — causal loop and stock and flow diagrams operationally, rule maps at collective-choice, dialogue and constitutions at the top.
## The formal upgrade

For older students, the ADICO grammar from Crawford and Ostrom. Every rule statement decomposes into Attribute, who it applies to; Deontic, may or must or must not; aIm, the action; Condition, when and where; and Or-else, the sanction.

The investigative payoff is immediate. In real documents the or-else slot is almost always empty. A statement with no or-else is not a rule, it is a norm or a shared strategy. So the first mechanical move on any ordinance, permit, policy or charter is to find the or-else. No or-else, no enforcement, and the rules in use will drift immediately and predictably. A student with a highlighter and ADICO can work through a town code in an afternoon and find things a reporter would miss. It also makes rules machine-comparable, which is what a rule map needs.
## Mapping rules rather than actors
Every stakeholder map ever drawn puts people in circles. Nobody draws the sediment the people leave behind.

A rule graph has rules as nodes. An ordinance, a permit condition, a statute rider, a board policy, a deed restriction, a union clause, an unwritten we-always-do-it-this-way. The edges are authorises, constrains, delegates, supersedes, exempts, funds, triggers, sunsets. Three horizontal bands hold the three levels, and an edge crossing bands upward is a rule reaching above its station, which is the interesting case.
Four properties make it more than a picture.

- Provenance. Every rule carries who made it, at which level, and when, so the rule graph and the timeline are one object seen two ways. Rules have birthdays and most have no death date.
- Two kinds of effect edge, in two colours. Intended effect, taken from the rule's own preamble, and observed effect, taken from measurement. A rule whose observed edges do not overlap its intended edges has drifted. A rule with intended edges and no observed edges was never enforced. A rule with observed edges nobody mentioned is the unintended consequence, now visible as a shape rather than an anecdote.
- Rules are a stock. Draw the stock and flow: rule-making inflow, repeal outflow. In most institutions the repeal valve is missing or has an area near zero, so the stock only grows. Where is the repeal valve is a question a fourteen-year-old can ask a town council, and it is devastating.
- The aggregator. Tag every decision with the aggregation rule actually used — majority, supermajority, consensus, consent, unanimity, single authority, default by inaction, whoever showed up.

Reading the town's rules is practised by maintaining our own. Each activity writes a one-page constitution using the seven rule types and amends it in public, so the school runs its own rule graph with its own sediment, its own drifted clauses and its own missing repeal valve. Students will find their own dead rules faster than the town's, which is the honest order. See [[Constitution Of The Gap Desk]].
*Marc Pierson and Claude Opus 5 · September 2026*

story.text: Investigative journalism is substantially about the gap between rules in form and rules in use, and that gap is the spine of the Foothills Outlook as a hub rather than a stream. It is also the same instrument the school turns on itself, in [[Curriculum Is A Record]].
## The gap is the spine

The canonical accountability story has four beats. Here is what the rule promised. Here is what happened. Here is the distance between them. Here is who benefits from the distance being maintained. Building codes against what got built. A consent decree against practice. Permit conditions against actual monitoring. Procurement rules against contracts awarded. Once you see the shape you cannot unsee it.
## But it is not the whole body
Three genres fall outside it, and a paper that only does gaps becomes a prosecutor's office.

- Rule against rule. Not form against use but form against form — two rules in conflict, or a rule at one level quietly voiding one below it. A rider attached to a must-pass bill is exactly this, and gap analysis cannot see it because nothing was violated.
- No rule at all. The harm that is entirely legal. Often the bigger story, and structurally invisible to a gap ledger because there is no form to compare the use against. It was all legal may be the most valuable sentence a small-town paper can print.
- Witness. What it is like. Not a gap but a presence. Necessary, and the thing students do better than professionals, because people talk to children.
So four beats for the Outlook: the Gap, the Collision, the Legal Harm, and the Witness.
## The ledger

The paper's primary artifact is not articles. It is a standing ledger in the wiki, one entry per rule, carrying the rule text, its source, what it promises, what was measured, the delta, the status as open or closed or disputed or answered, who is accountable, and the date of the last check. Articles are updates to entries. The front page carries the top open gaps and how long each has been open.
That makes local journalism cumulative, which it almost never is. A story today does not vanish next week, it becomes a line that stays open until somebody closes it.

It also hooks into everything else. Each entry's rule is a node in the rule graph described in [[Seven Questions]]. Each measurement is a control chart series. Each contested entry gets its left and right polygons in the ecology, institutions and politics frame. Each gets a place on the timeline.
## Four rules before the first issue
Superior is 2,400 people and everyone is somebody's cousin, so a gap ledger can become a pillory.

- The subject is the rule, not the person. Entries are titled by ordinance, not by name.
- Right of reply is structural. Every entry carries a reply field the subject can fill, published in the same place with the same weight, rather than a letter to the editor three weeks later.
- The school publishes its own gaps first, in the same ledger, in the same format — its constitutions against its practice. That is what buys the standing to publish anyone else's, and nothing else will.
- Whoever asks answers. A student collecting an oral history or an interview answers the same questions they ask, because trust exists only where the exchange is reciprocal. This is the fifth principle of plática, and the reason our interviews are not extraction. See [[Campfire Not Bonfire]].
## Three tempos
Paper, weekly or monthly, because the elders read paper and paper gets left on a table. It carries the current drawing and the open questions.
Wiki, continuous, holding the history and the forks.
The wall, physical, in the library or the old hotel or the co-op, with pens attached. This is the one everyone forgets, and it is where the arguing actually happens.

Every recurring town conversation — water, the mine, the highway, the clinic, the school — gets a standing page, a standing drawing and a standing slot in the paper. Journalism here means maintaining the drawings rather than producing takes, and the measure of a good issue is that the drawing got better.
*Marc Pierson and Claude Opus 5 · September 2026*

## Boundary

Anyone who has earned Verify and signed this page. You join by shadowing two entries and then verifying one under a Signer. You leave by saying so at any circle: your name comes off, your entries stay. No one is removed except by the amendment procedure below.
## Position

Four roles, held temporarily and never by the same person twice running. Checker does the verification. Signer is an adult who countersigns before publication, at least one, always named on the entry. Keeper maintains the ledger and is the only role that may change an entry's status. Reply Holder carries the draft to its subject, in person, before publication.
## Choice

A Checker may open an entry, gather, measure and draft, and may not publish. A Signer may publish and may refuse, and a refusal is written on the entry with its reason. A Keeper may change status and may not change findings. The Reply Holder must deliver the draft in person and may not publish before the reply window closes. No one may open an entry about a household they live in. Whoever asks answers: a Checker conducting an interview answers the same questions they ask.
## Aggregation

Opening an entry takes any two members. Publishing takes the Checker plus one Signer with the reply window closed. Moving an entry to closed takes the Keeper plus the subject's acknowledgement, or two Signers if the subject will not respond. Amending this page takes consent, meaning no sustained objection after one full circle of speaking.
## Information

Every entry shows the rule text, its source, who checked, what was measured, when, and the reply. Sources are named unless the Desk grants anonymity, and the granting is recorded even when the name is not. Drafts are open to the whole Desk and nothing is confidential from the Desk. The Desk's own failures go in the ledger like anyone else's.
## Payoff

Badges are Verify, Measure, Interview, Edit and Keep. Bylines are real names. The cost is that your name is on it: if it is wrong, you write the correction and you sign it. No entry is opened for money, and the Desk takes no advertising from the subject of an open entry.
## Scope

The Desk may publish about rules, institutions and public decisions. It may never publish about a minor's health or discipline, anyone's immigration status, or a household's finances. This clause may be amended to be stricter but never looser. Entries about this school have the same standing as any other.
## Amendment

Any member may propose, in writing, on this page. One full circle of speaking, then the consent rule above. The old version stays in history with the reason for the change written in. This page is reviewed every season whether or not anyone proposes anything, and reviewed includes asking of each clause whether it has quietly become a rule in form only.
## Two things to notice

The Scope clause has a ratchet — stricter but never looser. That is an entrenchment device, and it is how a minor is protected from a future membership that no longer remembers why the clause exists. No aggregation rule gets around it.

The Amendment clause audits itself for the same gap the Desk audits in everyone else. A constitution that never checks whether it is still in use is exactly the sediment we are teaching students to find.

story.text: A theory and practice of holding hard conversations that do not escalate, and that do not abandon the shared drawing for war paint. The constitution that governs one is in [[Constitution Of The Gap Desk]]. This page is sourced; the earlier draft was written from memory and got several things wrong.
## What turns a campfire into a bonfire

- A decision attaches to the talk. The moment something is at stake in this conversation, advocacy displaces inquiry. This is the primary cause.
- An audience appears. Recording, press, somebody posting. People begin speaking to the absent third party rather than to each other.
- Speaking turns become scarce, and competition for the floor begins.
- Identity is threatened, and the shared drawing is claimed by one side as its banner. That is the war paint moment: the drawing stops being a common object and becomes a flag.
- Time is compressed. Short meetings escalate.
## What Bohm gives and what he does not

Formal Bohmian dialogue supplies the cognitive discipline. Suspension, which means holding an assumption out in front of you where you and others can see it, neither suppressing it nor acting from it. Proprioception of thought. No agenda, no decision, a circle, a facilitator who fades.

It is powerful and it is culturally thin. A circle of strangers with no entry ritual, no relationship before the room and no obligation after it, and explicitly no purpose. That works in a seminar. In a town where everyone will see each other at the grocery store tomorrow it is the wrong model.
## Two talanoa lineages, which are not the same thing
They are routinely conflated and they came from different places for different purposes. Keeping them apart matters for us, because it is the first one we actually want.

Sitiveni Halapua, a Tongan development economist and then director of the East-West Center's Pacific Islands Development Program, developed the talanoa process for political mediation. He used it during the Cook Islands economic collapse of 1996, in Fiji's reconciliation after the May 2000 coup, and in ethnic reconciliation meetings in the Solomon Islands. The Fiji work ran as five two-day sessions plus smaller working sessions between November 2000 and July 2002, drawing in political opponents, religious leaders, former hostages and coup sympathisers, and eventually the leaders of both main ethnic parties, who agreed to form standing committees on land and constitutional reform.

Timote Vaioleti, an academic of Tongan ancestry, separately picked up talanoa as a research methodology, arguing in 2006 for an appropriate approach to researching Pacific educational and social issues in Aotearoa. That is the lineage most of the academic literature follows.
The political lineage is the one closest to what a Superior fire circle needs, and Halapua's own framing is better than anything in our earlier draft.
## Halapua's rules, which correct ours
Talanoa proceeds without any predetermined expectations for agreement. In Halapua's words, to say people have to agree to something is starting at the wrong end.
The aim is understanding rather than agreement. Living with the differences, and understanding them better, is a good start.
Participants set their own ground rules, and in Fiji those were inclusion, reconciliation and mutual respect.

The process deliberately takes the issue out of the arena where points are scored. Prime Minister Qarase described it as taking the issues away from debate in parliament, away from scoring political points and glossing over issues.

That last one vindicates our design rule but states it better. The rule is not that no decision may ever be made at a campfire. The rule is that the campfire is not the arena where the decision is won, and nobody arrives owing anybody agreement.
## Vā, and why it is the thing being protected

Vā is the space or the relationship between people — in Melani Anae's phrase, the sacred, spiritual and social spaces of human relationships. In Tongan, vā is the distance between or distance apart, and tauhi means to look after or tend, so tauhi vā is the nurturing of sociospatial ties, as Tēvita Kaili set out in The Contemporary Pacific in 2005. The Samoan form is teu le vā, which Anae wrote on in 2010.

Vā is what Bohm has no word for, and it reframes the whole problem. The reason a fire must not become a bonfire is not that heat is bad. It is that the vā is the thing that has to still be there afterwards. A community will accept that statement of the rule because it names what they are already protecting.
The cultivation of vā in talanoa aims at understanding rather than agreement, and thereby at information that is true or authentic — moʻoni. When it goes well it produces mālie and māfana.
## Kakala, and the project arc

Konai Helu Thaman introduced kakala, the Tongan garland, as a framework in 1992, with three stages: toli, tui and luva. Seuula Johansson-Fua — Tongan, Director of the Institute of Education at the University of the South Pacific, and convenor of the Rethinking Pacific Education Initiative — expanded it to six components in her 2014 chapter Kakala Research Framework: A Garland in Celebration of a Decade of Rethinking Education, in Of Waves, Winds and Wonderful Things, adding teu and incorporating mālie and māfana from Linitā Manuatu's Auckland theses of 2000 and 2001.

- Teu — preparation. Conceptualising, designing and planning, and examining your own position before beginning.
- Toli — the selection and collection of flowers. Who is included, how, and with what ethics. The ethics at this stage are what make the gathering authentic rather than merely complete.
- Tui — weaving the garland. Analysis and composition. Johansson-Fua describes it as collective work between the older women who string the kakala and the young girls sent out for flowers, with the pattern changing and being negotiated and corrected between them as it goes.
- Luva — the presentation of the finished garland. Giving a gift with heartfelt sincerity, humility and honour, carrying the knowledge that much time, work and sacrifice went into it. In research it is the giving back of the findings to the people they came from.
- Mālie — an expression of appreciation, in performance the word the audience calls out, and in the framework the judgement that what has been presented is of high quality, monitored against utility, applicability and relevance to the context. Manuatu conceptualises it as energy that moves and transforms, draws on passion and uplifts the heart.
- Māfana — warmth. The heartfelt feeling that causes an emotional reaction in everyone involved.

Two things follow directly for us. Luva is the graduation requirement, said better than we said it: a thing left behind is a gift given with sincerity and honour, and the giving is the completion rather than the keeping. And mālie and māfana are better conversation measures than any count of steelmanned arguments, because a community can judge them without training. Keep a behavioural count as well, but the felt measure is the real one.
## Vanua, which may fit Superior better than talanoa

Vanua is a universal whole with four interrelated dimensions — physical, social, cultural and spiritual — covering land, people, chiefs, knowledge, relationships and spirituality together.

Its value here is that it is a protocol rather than a disposition. Plan, seek permission from the vanua, talanoa, gift appropriately, and report back — and the result is a lifelong connection between the researcher and the researched rather than a completed transaction. A school sending students to ask their neighbours questions needs exactly that arc, and it maps onto teu, toli, tui and luva without strain.
Nabobo-Baba and Farrelly also note that talanoa has formal and instrumental forms as well as informal ones; the Fijian formal register is veivosaki.
## The critique we should take seriously

Laumua Tunufai's Pacific Research: Rethinking the Talanoa Methodology, in New Zealand Sociology in 2016, argues that talanoa is best regarded as a research method rather than a methodology, because it lacks the philosophical rationale and the processual clarity that kakala and vanua unambiguously have.
He makes three points that land directly on what we are doing.

- Deconstructing talanoa into tala and noa is a Tongan move. Vaioleti glosses tala as tale, relate, story, tell or declare, and noa as common, old, of no value, without thought, without exertion, nothingness, empty — so talanoa literally becomes talking about nothing in particular. Tunufai accepts this within the Tongan context and argues it is counterproductive elsewhere, and asks pointedly how talking about nothing yields more authentic and trustworthy data.
- The pan-Pacific claim is inconsistent with decolonisation's own emphasis on local relevance. Talanoa is borrowed or foreign for most Pacific nations, and in Samoan the deliberations of titled and elderly people are properly fa'afaletui rather than talanoa at all.
- What talanoa claims to do differently could also be achieved by other methods, of which talanoa may be a nice translation. The point of departure is the cultural qualification and sensitivity of the person holding the conversation, not the name of the method.

That third point is the one aimed at us. If we import the word and not the substance, we have done precisely the thing the literature warns against, and we will have taken a name from people who are still fighting to keep it meaning something.
## Plática, which is Superior's own

The Chicana and Latina tradition of plática is structurally close and locally at home. Edén Fierros and Dolores Delgado Bernal formalised it in Vamos a Platicar: The Contours of Pláticas as Chicana/Latina Feminist Methodology, in Chicana/Latina Studies in 2016, drawing on the curandera Elena Avila, who defines a plática as a deep heart-to-heart talk that continues for as long as it needs, and who says the most important ingredient in the plática is trust.
Their five principles.

- It draws on Chicana and Latina feminist theory, and on other critical theory that centres people the system has treated as marginal.
- It is relational, honouring participants as co-constructors of knowledge rather than sources of it, grounded in respeto for the contributor as a holder and creator of knowledge.
- It connects everyday lived experience to the inquiry rather than minimising it. Conversations that begin about school quickly include family, language, sex and gender, and that is the method working rather than drifting.
- It provides a potential space for healing.
- It relies on reciprocity, vulnerability and the researcher's own reflexivity. Trust exists only if the exchange is reciprocal, so the researcher must be willing to share what they ask of others. Unlike an interview, where the questioner says as little as possible, a plática talks back and forth.

That fifth principle converts straight into a rule for us: a student collecting an oral history answers the same questions they ask. No one-way extraction. It is the single most concrete thing this reading produced and it should go into the newsroom constitution in [[Gap Ledger]].
## The integration, restated

Kakala supplies the project arc, and vanua supplies the protocol for entering a community that is not yours. Talanoa supplies the conversation form, in Halapua's political register rather than the research one. Vā names the thing being protected. Mālie and māfana are the evaluation. Bohm's suspension is one technique used inside the conversation rather than the frame around it. Plática is the local tradition that already carries most of this in Spanish, and it is not borrowed.

Food and setting are not decoration. In a documented talanoa with students, participants hesitated to eat when the setting still felt like an academic one, and relaxed when it did not. The entry ritual is doing real work, and a room that reads as institutional defeats it.
## The caution, which is load bearing

Importing a Pacific framework wholesale into an Arizona copper town, over the top of Apache and Mexican-American communities who have their own practices, would be the exact colonial move these scholars write against — and Tunufai's critique says so about Pacific peoples borrowing from each other, let alone us.

The honest version is three sided. Bring talanoa, kakala and vanua in named, cited and credited as someone else's work. Lead locally with plática, which is already Superior's. And treat Apache council practice as a conversation to be had rather than a literature to be reviewed, because it is not ours to characterise.

Putting plática, talanoa and Apache practice beside each other and finding the shared structure is itself the lesson, and it is the strongest possible demonstration that the school's frameworks are not the school's property.

Edén Fierros and Dolores Delgado Bernal formalised it in Vamos a Platicar: The Contours of Pláticas as Chicana/Latina Feminist Methodology, in Chicana/Latina Studies in 2016, drawing on the curandera Elena Avila, who defines a plática as a deep heart-to-heart talk that continues for as long as it needs, and who says the most important ingredient in the plática is trust.
Their five principles.

- It draws on Chicana and Latina feminist theory, and on other critical theory that centres people the system has treated as marginal.
- It is relational, honouring participants as co-constructors of knowledge rather than sources of it, grounded in respeto for the contributor as a holder and creator of knowledge.
- It connects everyday lived experience to the inquiry rather than minimising it. Conversations that begin about school quickly include family, language, sex and gender, and that is the method working rather than drifting.
- It provides a potential space for healing.
- It relies on reciprocity, vulnerability and the researcher's own reflexivity. Trust exists only if the exchange is reciprocal, so the researcher must be willing to share what they ask of others. Unlike an interview, where the questioner says as little as possible, a plática talks back and forth.

That fifth principle converts straight into a rule for us: a student collecting an oral history answers the same questions they ask. No one-way extraction. It is the single most concrete thing this reading produced and it should go into the newsroom constitution in [[Gap Ledger]].
## The integration, restated

Kakala supplies the project arc, and vanua supplies the protocol for entering a community that is not yours. Talanoa supplies the conversation form, in Halapua's political register rather than the research one. Vā names the thing being protected. Mālie and māfana are the evaluation. Bohm's suspension is one technique used inside the conversation rather than the frame around it. Plática is the local tradition that already carries most of this in Spanish, and it is not borrowed.

Food and setting are not decoration. In a documented talanoa with students, participants hesitated to eat when the setting still felt like an academic one, and relaxed when it did not. The entry ritual is doing real work, and a room that reads as institutional defeats it.
## The caution, which is load bearing

Importing a Pacific framework wholesale into an Arizona copper town, over the top of Apache and Mexican-American communities who have their own practices, would be the exact colonial move these scholars write against — and Tunufai's critique says so about Pacific peoples borrowing from each other, let alone us.

The honest version is three sided. Bring talanoa, kakala and vanua in named, cited and credited as someone else's work. Lead locally with plática, which is already Superior's. And treat Apache council practice as a conversation to be had rather than a literature to be reviewed, because it is not ours to characterise.

Putting plática, talanoa and Apache practice beside each other and finding the shared structure is itself the lesson, and it is the strongest possible demonstration that the school's frameworks are not the school's property.

story.text: How the NDC school sits next to the existing public schools without triggering the conflict, and how credit eventually flows both ways. The strategy is peripheral participation and adaptive adoption rather than confrontation, and it generalises past the school to every other department of local government.
## Name the conflict before it names you

Funding is the real one and everything else is downstream. Arizona district money follows average daily membership, and in a small district anything that looks like it pulls students pulls dollars. Hence the commitment in [[NDC School Superior]]: never enrol, never seek a charter, never apply for ADM funding.
The rest, honestly.

- Teacher status. Community mentors doing teacher-shaped work without certification reads as deprofessionalisation. The counter is that we badge what the district does not teach, and mentors are framed as the thing teachers chronically lack — a supply of expert adults — rather than as substitutes.
- Liability. Minors off campus, near a creek, near a mine. Real, boring, solvable, and it has to be solved before anyone will say yes to anything else.
- Accountability optics. The district is judged on test scores, graduation rate and chronic absenteeism. If we do not help those numbers we are a curiosity, and if we appear to hurt them we are an enemy.
- Political exposure. Anything touching Resolution is radioactive for a board elected by both sides. The [[Gap Ledger]] will eventually produce an entry somebody on the board hates, and that day should be planned for now rather than then.
## What the district needs and cannot get

- Career and technical education hours and work-based learning, funded in Arizona and impossible for a small district to staff.
- Evidence artifacts. A well log analysis is a science standard and an oral history is an English language arts standard. Districts need artifacts for their own reporting and have no time to generate them.
- Community engagement, demanded by every grant application and beyond the capacity of a district this size.
- Electives. Small schedules cannot be filled. This is the softest entry point and the most underrated.
- Chronic absenteeism, the metric every district is desperate about. A student who will not come to second period will show up for the map crew, and that is a fact the district can use.
## Four rungs, never skipped

- Rung zero, invisible. Weekends, after school, summer. No credit sought, no permission needed, nothing to say yes or no to. About a year. The only success condition is that individual teachers begin referring students unprompted. Rung zero also has to produce a record the institution does not yet know it needs, because a rung one that rests only on enthusiasm does not survive a summer — see the Ferndale outcome in [[Ferndale Ideal Education Model]].
- Rung one, one teacher of record. A single willing teacher accepts NDC work as evidence for their own assignment — the water dataset as the lab report, the oral history as the research paper. No policy, no board vote, no memorandum. The practice enters through a person, which is peripheral participation working on the institution the same way it works on a learner.
- Rung two, elective and technical credit by portfolio. Under mechanisms that already exist: independent study, work-based learning, technical education hours, demonstrated-competency credit. A written agreement and a board consent item rather than a policy rewrite. The badge ledger is the evidence package.
- Rung three, two-way transfer. District courses appear as badges on the ledger and NDC badges appear on the transcript. The membrane opens both directions and the district now has something to lose if the ledger stops existing. This is the rung where they start asking us for things.
- Rung four, adoption. The district runs its own version. Our job is to be copied and to be gracious about it. Success looks like the distinction dissolving.
Each rung is entered because somebody inside wants it, not because we proposed it. The proposal's job at every rung is to state something already obviously true to the person reading it.
## The translation layer
A badge ledger has to render as a transcript line without anyone at the district learning our vocabulary.

Every badge carries a state standard alignment code, estimated hours, an evidence link, the mentor's identifier, the date, and the see-do-teach level. A credit bundle is a named set of badges a counsellor can accept as half or one Carnegie unit. Rasch sets where the bundle's threshold sits on the ruler, but the counsellor never sees a logit. They see that a standard is met, with the hours, the portfolio and a named mentor's signature.

The ledger speaks Carnegie units and standard codes at its edge and Rasch in its interior. That is the whole diplomatic technique in one sentence, and it generalises to every other institution we eventually want to reach.
## The same ladder for local government
The long strategy has the identical shape, and the mechanism at every rung is the same: be the custodian of a record the institution needs and does not have. Not advocacy — custody.

Keep the creek record nobody asked for. One person inside starts citing it. It becomes an input to an official process — a public comment, a board packet, a grant narrative. Then the department maintains it. At that point the department's information flow has changed, which is Meadows leverage point six, reached without ever having fought at level three.
An institution will eventually adopt a record it has come to depend on, and adopting it changes how it sees.
## The risk, stated plainly
Capture runs both ways. If the district adopts the ledger, the district will want to control the ledger, and the entries about the district will be the first thing to quietly disappear.

The protections are self-custodied identity, so a learner holds credentials no institution can revoke, and forking, so that any version of the ledger with entries missing is visibly a fork rather than the record. Both have to be designed in at rung zero. At rung three it is too late to add them.
*Marc Pierson and Claude Opus 5 · September 2026*

story.text: Where each RCN tool lands, arranged by the five planes in [[NDC School Superior]] rather than as an inventory.
## Commons — what is out there

- RCN Map is the spine. Geology, water, land status across Forest Service, State Trust, private and tribal, historic structures, oral history pins, plant occurrences from the arboretum, heat and shade, the projected subsidence footprint. Every student adds layers, and over a decade this becomes the town's most valuable asset and belongs to the town.
- Issue Polygon Map holds parcels, ownership, the land exchange boundary, and the geographic version of the left and right polygons.
- RCN Timeline runs from the 1870s to now, boom and bust, with Allen relations so that during the strike and after the strike become arguable claims rather than loose phrasing. Students verify every date against the town's own records, and that verification is the history course.
- The substrate and its Layer 1 static projections give one graph and many lenses with no server. Each site is its own substrate, sealed and verifiable offline, which is the right architecture for a town with patchy connectivity.
## Practices — the repeated moves

- Graph tool in causal loop mode, from about age seven. Two arrows and a story: more of this, more of that; more of this, less of that. Reinforcing is a snowball and balancing is a thermostat. Starter loops come from town life — more mine jobs, more people, more stores, more reason to stay; fewer people, a smaller school, fewer reasons to stay; more pumping, a lower water table, deeper wells, higher cost, less pumping.
- Stock and flow mode once stock and flow can be held apart, around eleven or twelve. Bathtub first, then real bathtubs: the town water tank, the creek, enrolment, the stock of rules. Export to XMILE, simulate, be wrong, revise.
- Vester's impact matrix on a dozen town variables, sorting levers from indicators. A one-day exercise that reorganises how a room thinks.
- Ecology, institutions and politics mode for what a law actually does. A statute lands in politics, deforms an institution, and the institution's operations hit the ecology, and the interesting arrows are the slow return paths. Each side of a dispute builds its own full picture and only what both put there goes in the centre. The centre starts small and grows slowly, and the point is that the disagreement becomes precise and stays legitimate instead of being papered over.
- Neighbourhood risk management and Tripod Beta after any real incident — a flood, a mine accident, a fire, a near miss at the crossing. Real incident analysis, done properly, by teenagers.
- Object process methodology for structure without arithmetic, with the Odum coupling for value flows.
- Odum money counterflow for copper out and dollars in, and then the second circuit: where those dollars go inside town and how fast they leak. A measurable number and a good project.
- Wardley mapping with rent band analysis for older students — where the town's economy sits on the evolution axis, what is being rented from it, and what is genuinely commodity.
- Linkage of processes for the school as a system, drawn by the people inside it.
- Statistical process control on the creek gauge, the rain gauge, the well levels, the air monitor, clinic visits, and the quality of the town's conversations. A town that keeps its own control charts argues differently.
- The Rasch tool for the ruler and the Wright map, which is the transcript. See [[Curriculum Is A Record]].
- Bias Checker, run on the school's own journalism before it goes out.
- A3 as every project's one-page discipline.
- Graph Composer for the same picture at family, schema, variable and instance level, which is how a seven-year-old and a seventeen-year-old work on the same drawing at different grain.
## Record — what persists

- See one do one teach one is the journal of the learning journey. A self-custodied identifier minted on the student's own device and never held by the school. Every badge is a signed credential naming the learner, the mentor, the artifact and the date, producing a transparent chain of who learned what from whom that the student carries out the door and the school cannot revoke or lose. In a town where the district might close, that portability is not a nicety.
- FedWiki holds everything, forkable — curricula, drawings, oral histories, the rule graph, the constitutions.
- The rcngraph, rcntable and rcnoutliner plugins keep diagrams editable in place rather than flattened into pictures. A drawing nobody can edit has already stopped being a campfire object.
- MORE Outliner for thinking in structure before it becomes a diagram.
- Shared Care Plan and Groove for the health strand, and for a town with no hospital.
- Wiki Café for hosting, and for the pattern of a site per person.
## Arenas and Constitution

Arenas are mostly not tools. Outside is the default, rooms are named for what is made in them, and the fire circle needs food and a talking piece more than software. The constitutional plane needs only the wiki's page history, which is what makes an amendment visible, and the one-page template in [[Constitution Of The Gap Desk]].
*Marc Pierson and Claude Opus 5 · September 2026*

story.text: The generator behind [[Ferndale Ideal Education Model]]. Marc Pierson's self-certification protocol, published as [[Systems Certification]] on relocalizecreativity.net. One hour, alone, with three or four sheets of paper and a pencil. Do not read ahead.
## The protocol

- Step 1 — Think of an area of present concern and care. It does not matter what, only that it is really meaningful to you personally. Take your time. Be sure it is a big deal to you.
- Step 2 — List anything that comes to mind about it. A list, not an essay. Any thing — idea, person, place, object. At least fifteen items, and no more than fits on one sheet. You should feel that a lot of the stuff related to the topic is on the page.
- Step 3 — Choose about eight of them. You choose. Write those onto a clean sheet with lots of white space, and draw a border around each one.
- Step 4 — Draw lines connecting some of them, in ways that make sense to you. The connections must matter to you.
- Step 5 — Label the connecting lines. What does the line mean.
- Step 6 — Add arrowheads.
- Step 7 — If a line has two arrowheads, erase one and draw a second line to carry it.
- Step 8 — Make sure every line label is a verb that conveys action or change, typically ending in -ing. Expect to erase and redo some. You can rename the nodes at any time. This is your graph, your drawing, about something you care about.
- Step 9 — Read the graph aloud. Say only what is written on the page. If you used verbs you can do this; if you did not, you will find the verbs while trying.
- Step 10 — You have created a clear sparse visual story from thin air, from your own mind and experience. Now go back to Step 1 and recall how you felt when you were asked to do it. Say it out loud, listen to what you say, and write down what you just heard yourself say. Then do the same for every step. This takes about as long as making the drawing did.
- Step 11 — Make sure each step has a note recording how it felt and what you understood there. What have you learned. What could you do with this little graph. Was it interesting, fun, useful.
Only after all eleven, below a fold, does the protocol tell you what you demonstrated.
## What the design is actually doing

Everyone does it alone, first. The group work comes only after each person holds a finished drawing of their own. That is the opposite of how a facilitated workshop usually runs, and it is why the resulting map is federated rather than consensual — it is n personal drawings merged, with the seams still visible.

Step 2 sets a floor and a ceiling in the same breath: at least fifteen, no more than one page. The floor defeats the person who would write three things and stop. The ceiling defeats the person who would write forever rather than choose.

Authorship is handed back at every single step, explicitly. You pick the topic. You choose the eight. The connections must matter to you. This is your graph, your drawing, about something you care about. Nothing is assigned and nothing is marked.

Step 7 is the only formal discipline imposed anywhere in the protocol, and it is a real one: a line with two arrowheads is two relations pretending to be one, so it gets split. That single rule is what turns a doodle into a graph.

Step 8 is the hinge. Forcing verbs is what makes Step 9 possible, and Step 9 is the certification moment — reading the thing aloud proves to the person that they built a story rather than a decoration. Nobody else has to confirm it.

Steps 10 and 11 are half the protocol by time, and they are entirely about affect. Where the big learning is, in the protocol's own words. Every step page carries a Notes field, so the recording surface is present from the first minute rather than bolted on at the end.
## Why it works on people that school has failed
The Ferndale cohort was eighteen students who had given up on schooling and were invited back without a classroom. For that population every design choice above is load bearing.

A student who has learned that school is a place where other people choose the topic, set the length, and mark the result meets a protocol in which they choose the topic, the length is bounded by a sheet of paper, and nobody marks anything. The artifact at Step 9 is proof, produced by them, that they can do a thing they had been told for years they could not do.
And Step 10 asks them to look straight at the feelings that taught them otherwise. The drawing is the evidence; the recall is the diagnosis. Both belong to the learner.
## The nine natural cognitive skills

What the protocol says you demonstrated, once you have done it: focusing; listing, which is looking about, imagining, naming and limiting; culling, which is narrowing and selecting; arraying, which is spatial organising; connecting, which is formally relating; assigning direction, which is vectoring; labelling, which is clarifying; narrating; and reflecting and synthesising.

The point of the list is that every item on it is something the person was already doing before anyone taught them anything. The protocol does not install a skill, it names one. That is what makes self-certification an honest word rather than a soft one, and it is why the list stays hidden behind a fold until the work is done.

In our terms each of the nine is an item on the ruler, and each has a see, a do and a teach threshold. The whole protocol is one badge at do level and a much harder badge at teach level, because walking somebody else through Step 10 without rushing them is genuinely difficult.
## Concept map or causal loop

As written, the eleven steps produce a semantic network rather than a causal loop diagram. Step 2 invites any thing — idea, person, place, object — and Step 8 asks for action verbs, which yields propositions like teachers supporting the learning of science. The Ferndale map is exactly that, and so are its best lines: heartbreak envies love.

A causal loop diagram needs something different. The nodes must be variables that can be more or less, and the arrows carry a sign rather than a verb. Marc and Kerry Turner now start groups with causal loop diagrams instead, which for most adults is right and faster.
It is worth being clear about the trade, because the school needs both doors.

The verb version asks for no abstraction at all and pays off at Step 9 with a sentence anybody can say out loud. Teachers support the learning of science is a sentence. Teachers, arrow, science, plus is not. For someone who has been failed by school, that readable sentence is the entire point of the exercise and a variable is already one abstraction too many.

The causal loop version gets to feedback, which is where the systems insight actually lives, and the Ferndale map shows the cost of not getting there — fifty-four domain-level links, densely cyclic, none of them signed, so the loops are present and invisible.

The recommendation is a Step 12 rather than a different Step 1. Keep the eleven as the first drawing. Then convert: keep only the nodes that can be more or less, restate each verb as same direction or opposite direction, and look for a loop. The learner ends with the same care rendered two ways, which is itself the lesson about representation, and nobody has to start by being abstract.
Which door a person comes through should depend on the person, not the house style.
## The table discipline

The person who tends the table does not look at the work. Marc said in advance that he would not look, and then did not, and sat doing his own unrelated work while each person drew. When a section was finished he explained the next step. People asked, repeatedly, for more help, and he gave none beyond what is written above.
